title: What teams get wrong about B2B intent signals
summary: Reading competitor content puts a buyer in consideration, not in market. Here's why a B2B intent signal should build an ad audience first, and where sales fits.
body_markdown:
Perhaps it’s the word “intent” that steers a sales team wrong. The phrase is deceptively broad. Buyers show all sorts of[unique intent signals (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/platform/signals) in *every* stage of the funnel.


Yes, some of those leads are red hot and aching for an SDR to call them up. But many others just learned your company’s name for the first time and they’re not ready to chat.


When you respond to sophisticated data with blunt force tactics, it’s a waste of time for everyone involved. Intent signals show you *when* to engage a lead (a.ka. now). Teams need to think more about *how* to engage.


## **SDRs don’t know when to play it cool**


It’s hard to play it cool when you’re constantly getting alert messages. Like, when a contact at a target account reads your competitor's article on Forbes: your signal feed catches it and an alert message lands in Slack.


Your SDR calls within the hour. The prospect has never heard of your company, barely remembers the article, and is off the phone in 90 seconds. (Even if they remember the article, this kind of rushed engagement can feel kinda creepy instead of attentive.) Two weeks later the account is cold, and someone on the team decides the intent data was junk.


Slow your roll there, tiger. Just because somebody looked your way doesn’t mean that it’s time to get down on bended knee.


### The data is fine but the response is not


SDRs should be working leads that have already been nurtured, or at least primed. They shouldn’t be working signals straight off the feed. Everything upstream of that, while someone is still forming an opinion, is exactly the part that doesn’t need a human on the phone.


Remember when sales teams used to nurture leads? Warm them up first? It takes time. The buying committee needs to see your brand enough times, in enough places, that a rep’s first call isn’t the first time anyone at the account has heard of the company.


Automated engagement can do that labor while sales reps focus on people who are actually ready to seal the deal.


## **Pipelines collapse when intent is oversimplified**


Most account stage models run some version of pipeline stages. They place a signal in a category like aware, interested, or considering. A research signal is one of the cleaner ways to watch an account move from aware into interested or considering. The signal indicates that a lead spent real attention on a topic next to what you sell. That’s worth acting on, y’all.


But wait, one q: what kind of action is warranted?


The strategy is to always be moving the right lead through the right stage, rather than putting the hard sell on every lead at once. Different stages require different engagement strategies.


Teams that have built a lot of ABM engines tend to land on the same conclusion: capturing signals was never the hard part; deciding what each one earns is. Activation is where nearly all the real work lives, and the qualification step is where signal fatigue starts. The programs that hold up reserve direct outreach for the highest-confidence signals and route everything else to targeting strategies.


### Engagement? Yes! Full-court press? No… no.


When someone’s researching your competitor, they’re in consideration mode, rather than purchase mode. The right first move for consideration-mode behavior is exposure.


For most signals that means creating an audience. Put targeted ads in front of them so that they can get to know your brand long before any sales folks get involved. It nurtures leads more effectively. It also keeps SDRs focused on deals they can actually close.


Prospecting into that warmer tier consistently converts several times better than starting cold.


## **Individualized data misses the forest for the trees**


Granular data is an incredible asset… One that sales teams tend to misuse.


The person reading that Forbes article is often a manager doing early homework for someone else. Focusing all of your[engagement tactics (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/what-to-do-with-intent-data) on them alone is a mistake. They’re part of a committee, alongside a handful of other people who also need to be persuaded (and haven’t heard of your company yet either).


The engagement strategy needs to focus on all of those people. Put the named contacts on that account’s buying committee into an audience and run ads to all of them, on LinkedIn, Google, and wherever else you already buy. Committees also churn, so audiences that update as people change roles hold together better than a list built by hand in March.


Rather than blasting one person and hoping that they relay the message to their peers, you have an entire set of buyers who are familiar with your content before anyone on your team says a word to them.


## **Signal, in excess, starts to feel like noise**


Signals arrive at machine volume. A team tracking site activity, competitor research, and content engagement across a few thousand target accounts will generate hundreds of alerts a week. Rep capacity covers a fraction of that, so the queue backs up and whatever does get worked gets worked badly.


There’s a slower cost underneath the obvious one. A rep who calls three cold research signals in a row and gets nowhere stops trusting the feed, and a few weeks after that stops opening it. You now own a signal system producing alerts that nobody reads, which is worse than owning none at all, because you paid for this one and built a process around it.


What you need is a better workflow, and rarely a better alert.


## **Behavioral data distracts from broader context**


Some signals genuinely mean that a lead is red hot and eager to chat with a sales rep. Those signals are almost always the outgrowth of existing relationships. It might be a lead your AE’s been working for months, or a recently closed-lost account.


Leads like these should never sit behind an ad sequence. A champion who changes jobs, for example, is one of the strongest possible leads. When their signals pop up in your CRM, it’s time to pick up the phone.


All of those other signals are merely invitations to *start* building a relationship.


### You can build relationships with a lighter touch


It takes time, of course, and steady, repeated engagement. That’s what software is for. Keep the accounts and named contacts in view, keep ads running against them as the signal builds, and let familiarity accumulate on its own schedule instead of forcing it in a 90-second call. By the time there’s a relationship worth having, sales isn’t starting from zero.


You can’t make these kinds of decisions until you have context on these relationships. Rating leads in terms of intensity doesn’t mean much without that context. When you have it, strategic questions start to answer themselves.


## **The wrong signal analysis shows up in QBR**


No matter how grateful the sales team might be for this data, you still have to defend your strategy before the stakeholders. Can you prove that any of this actually drove sales?


Speed to first touch is the metric most teams report. It’s tempting to boast about, and it often looks impressive on a chart, but it doesn’t prove results.


### You need data that connects to the bottom-line


The better questions are historical and aggregate:


-


What share of research signals became an ad-engaged contact?


-


How does the meeting rate from ad-touched contacts compare against contacts called cold out of the same feed?


-


How much pipeline traces back to committees your ads actually reached?


Hold 20 percent of your signals out and run them the old way for a quarter if you want that comparison to be honest. You’ll need those numbers because you’ll be asked for them.


A score you can’t interrogate doesn’t survive a QBR. Neither does an attribution model whose logic nobody in the room can follow. Being able to name which contacts your ads touched before a deal closed is what turns a signal program from an activity report into a case for more budget.

## **Frequently asked questions about intent signals**


### What’s an intent signal?


An intent signal is any observable behavior that suggests someone is researching your category. It might be a competitor-content view, a pricing-page visit, or a review-site read. It tells you attention is happening. It doesn’t tell you the person’s budget, timeline, or authority.


### Why shouldn't every intent signal trigger a sales call?


Because most signals put someone in consideration, not purchase mode, and a cold call assumes the opposite. A contact reading a competitor’s explainer is early in the process. They rarely own the decision. If you call them immediately then you’ve spent your best shot on the wrong buyer at the wrong stage. To the buyer it can read like surveillance instead of attentiveness.


### What should happen instead of a sales call?


The signal should build an ad audience around the account’s entire buying committee, not just the one contact who tripped it. That way the named people likely to be involved in the decision see your company repeatedly before anyone calls them. Sales gets involved once the committee has already formed an impression, not before.


### Which signals should still go straight to a rep?


Signals sitting on top of an existing relationship. An open opportunity your AE is already working. A closed-lost account inside 90 days. A champion changing jobs. All three justify same-day outreach, because the relationship already exists. A direct touch reads as attentive instead of intrusive.


### How does Vector act on intent signals differently?


Vector keeps the named contacts on a buying committee attached to the signal instead of letting them get lost in a company-level score. It builds an ad audience around those contacts as the account moves through consideration, and keeps that audience updated as the committee changes. Sales inherits a contact who’s already seen the company, plus a record of exactly which contacts were reached before the deal closed.
